les-01.q: How many real vowels does Tarifit have?
les-01.explain: Three real vowels (a, i, u). The schwa e does not count as a full vowel.

options: the Arabic ﻍ — a 'gh' sound as in Maghreb
pinching sound, deeper in the throat
k as deep as possible in the throat
les-01.explain: ɣ is the Arabic غ — a 'gh' sound, as in Maghreb or the soft Dutch g.

les-01.q: What is the difference between ḏ and ṯ?
options: ḏ is dark, ṯ is light
ḏ = th in this (voiced); ṯ = th in thin (voiceless)
they are identical, just written differently
ḏ comes first, ṯ comes last in a word
les-01.explain: Both have an underscore and are pronounced blowing — as in English this versus thin.

les-01.q: Match each guttural sound with its description.

pairs.right: k as deep as possible in the throat

les-01.q: The letter ř historically comes from a…
les-01.explain: In Tarifit the old l has become an r-like sound, written as ř. The double ll became ǧ.

les-01.q: The five dark consonants (dot below) are ḍ, ṣ, ṭ, ẓ and…
les-01.explain: ṛ is the dark variant of the regular r. The darkness colors the entire word.

les-01.q: Which letter is the voiced counterpart of x (the sharp throat-h)?
les-01.explain: ɣ and x are a voiced/voiceless pair — same mouth position, but ɣ involves vibration of the vocal cords.

les-01.q: What effect do dark consonants (ḍ, ṣ, ṭ, ẓ, ṛ) have on surrounding vowels?
options: They colour the surrounding vowels darker
They have no effect on vowels
les-01.explain: Dark consonants (recognisable by the dot underneath) colour surrounding vowels darker — a feature of pharyngalisation in Tarifit.

les-01.q: Which three forms are the real vowels of Tarifit?
les-01.explain: Tarifit has three real vowels: a, i and u. The schwa e is not a full vowel and has a different status.

les-02.q: What form do you use with a woman when you want to say 'you'?
les-02.explain: cemm against a woman, cekk against a man.
netta = he. nettaṯ = they — remember the difference at the end-ṯ.
The small particle ḏ does the work of 'is/am' here.

les-02.q: What form do you use for 'you' if the group consists entirely of women?
les-02.explain: kennint only for pure women groups; with one man added it automatically becomes knowledge.

les-02.q: Match each Tarifit pronoun with its meaning.
Which pronoun do you use for 'they' in the plural when the group consists exclusively of women?
les-02.explain: nitnenṯ is used for a group of exclusively women. For a mixed group or men, use nitni.

les-03.q: Fill in the missing particle: necc ? Mimun — 'I am Mimoun'.
les-03.explain: ḏ does the work of 'being' in non-verbal sentences: X · ḏ · Y.

les-03.q: Translate to Tarifit: 'he is a man'. (Hint: 'man' = āryaz.)

options: If what comes after is a noun
If what comes after is a prepositional phrase or adverb
les-03.explain: ḏ only appears before a noun or pronoun. For adverbs (such as ammu 'so'), ḏ is omitted: necc ammu.
ḏ necc — literally 'it is I'. With ḏ in front, the emphasis is on the predicate.

les-03.q: Translate to Tarifit: 'it's my brother'. (Hint: 'my brother' = uma.)
les-03.explain: ḏ uma — no separate pronoun for it, because uma has already ingrained 'my' (Class III, see next lesson).

les-03.q: The particle ḏ (copula) is never conjugated. What does that mean?
options: It changes with the gender of the subject
It always stays the same form, regardless of who the subject is
It has a plural form di
les-03.explain: ḏ is invariable — the same form for I, you, he, she, we. That makes it one of the simplest elements of Tarifit.

les-03.q: Which word order is correct for 'she is a woman'? (woman = ṯamɣārṯ)
les-03.explain: The order is: SUBJECT + ḏ + NOUN. So: nettaṯ ḏ ṯamɣārṯ = "she is a woman".
āryaz means "man". In the sentence netta ḏ āryaz = "he is a man", it functions as the predicate after ḏ.

les-04.q: Match each family word with its meaning.

options: your father (if you are talking to a man)
les-04.explain: Suffix -c = 'your (M)'. For a woman you would say baba-m.
Suffix -s covers both 'his' and 'her' — context determines which.
ɛzizi = paternal uncle. xari = maternal uncle. Tarifit always makes this distinction.

les-04.q: Which word does 'my' not automatically have in it?
les-04.explain: āryaz 'man' is a common Class-I noun. The other three are family words (Class III) with 'mine' built in.

les-04.q: Which suffix do you use for 'your' when speaking to a woman?
les-04.explain: Suffix -m = "your (F)". E.g. baba-m = "your father (when you are a woman)". The suffix -c is for male conversation partners.
Suffix -s covers both "his" and "her" — context determines which. yemma-s = "his/her mother".

les-04.q: Why does āryaz "man" not have a built-in "my", while baba does?
options: Because āryaz is a regular noun (Class I), not a kinship term
Because it is too long to add a suffix to
les-04.explain: baba, yemma and uma are kinship terms that already contain "my". āryaz is a regular noun without built-in possession.

les-05.q: What does aqq-ec mliḥ? literally mean?
les-05.explain: Literally 'are you good?' — a regular greeting in Riffian families.
waxxa is a common word of agreement in all Moroccan languages.

les-05.q: Complete: aɣ-am-? means 'here you have it (V)' (= offering of a thing to a woman).
les-05.explain: -ṯ is the direct object clitic 'it' (3SG:M). The order in aɣ-am-ṯ is: aɣ + indirect object (to you V) + direct object (it).
With ḏ in front you emphasize the predicate — 'it's me (and no one else)'.

les-05.q: Match each expression to its meaning.
What form of aɣ-… do you use with several men when you offer them something?
les-05.explain: -awem is the indirect-object clitic 'to you (M)'. -am = to you (F), -ac = to you (M), -as = to him/her.
aɣ-am = "here you go", addressed to a man. For a woman it is aɣ-am-ṯ, for several men aɣ-awem.

les-05.q: You want to say 'it's me' in Tarifit. Which form do you use?
les-05.explain: ḏ necc — with ḏ at the front, the emphasis falls on the predicate: "it is me (and no one else)".

les-05.q: Which word means 'okay' or 'agreed' in Tarifit?
les-05.explain: waxxa means "okay, agreed" and is a widely used expression of agreement.

les-06.q: Look up 'sitting' in a Tarifit dictionary. What shape do you expect there?
les-06.explain: Tarifit dictionaries take the imperative / bare stem as a keyword. Dutch dictionaries take the infinitive — Tarifit does not have it.

les-06.q: What is typical of the Tarifit conjugation compared to Dutch?
options: a prefix and a suffix around the stem
no personal form at all — context determines everything
exactly the same as in Arabic
les-06.explain: Many people get something on both sides: 'you sit' = ṯ- qqim-eḏ. Dutch only has suffixes ('you walk').

les-06.q: Tarifit verbs do not encode 'time', but…
les-06.explain: A verb says something about how the action is, not when. You express time with particles and context. You will dive deep into this in Lesson 09.
1SG = STEM + -eɣ. No prefix with 'I' — that's easy to remember.
3SG:M = y- + STEM. The e between y and q is an auxiliary vowel (schwa) that makes pronunciation easier.
Two clues: prefix ṯ- and suffix -eḏ. That combination belongs to 2SG ('you'), against both men and women.
There is a ṯ--prefix, but no -eḏ-suffix. That's 3SG:V ('they'). The difference with 'you' is therefore only in that suffix.

les-06.q: Link person and form for stem qqim 'sit':
les-06.explain: Five patterns, one stem. Once you know these, you can conjugate any standard verb — you'll do that in Lessons 07 and 08.

les-06.q: What is the form for "we sit" (stem qqim)?
les-06.explain: 1PL = n- + stem: neqqim. No suffix for "we".

les-06.q: Which person has no prefix in the Tarifit conjugation?
les-06.explain: Only "I" (1SG) has no prefix. The form is purely STEM + -eɣ, as in qqimeɣ "I sit".

les-06.q: What is the correct form for "they sit" (exclusively women, stem qqim)?
les-06.explain: 3PL:F = STEM + -enṯ: qqimenṯ. No prefix for the third person plural.

les-07.q: Which suffix belongs to ik in the standard pattern?
les-07.explain: 1SG (ik) does not get a prefix and the suffix -eɣ. -eḏ belongs to 2SG ('you'), -en to 3PL:M ('she M'), -em to 2PL:M ('you M').

les-07.q: What is the only difference between he and she (singular)?
options: a vowel change in the stem
the prefix: y- for he, ṯ- for she
the suffix: he gets -a, she gets nothing
they are identical — context determines meaning
les-07.explain: Both have no suffix; only the prefix differs. y- = male, ṯ- = female. You also encounter the same ṯ- with 'you' — there is a suffix behind it.

options: ṯ- as prefix and -eḏ as suffix
les-07.explain: 2SG is the only singular form with both a prefix (ṯ-) and a suffix (-eḏ). This makes it the easiest shape to recognize.
Stem ari + suffix -eɣ. The two i's merge in the spelling to form ariɣ.
Verbs that end in a vowel are given -iḏ (not -eḏ) as a 2SG suffix. This also applies to 'you' at cfa, wḏa etc.
Prefix y- + stem cc = yecc, with a schwa-e in between for pronunciation. In the Perfective, 'eat' gets an extra a: yecca 'he ate' (Lesson 09).
ṯ- + STEM + -eḏ is always 2SG. Works for men and women — Tarifit makes no distinction between 'you' here.
Prefix y- = 3SG:M. No suffix. Before 'she writes' it would read ṯari.

les-07.q: Match each pattern to its person:
les-07.explain: Four patterns for singular. Trick: 'I' has only suffix, 'he/she' only prefix, 'you' both.
3SG:M = y- + stem: ɣari. No suffix. For "she writes" it would be ṯari.
1PL = n- + stem: nari. The same pattern as neqqim "we sit".
1SG = stem + -iɣ: cciɣ. Note: necc means "I" (pronoun), cciɣ is the verb form.

les-08.q: What prefix does we have in neqqim?
les-08.explain: 1PL is the simplest: n- + STEM. No suffix. Same pattern as 3SG:M but with n- instead of y-.

les-08.q: When do you use the feminine-plural suffix -enṯ?
options: always in a group with more than two people
only if the group consists exclusively of women
les-08.explain: One man in the group? Then you fall back on the masculine form -em / -en. Comparable to French (elles becomes ils in mixed groups).

les-08.q: What is the difference between qqimen and ṯeqqimem?
options: meaning is identical, only spelling variant
the first is past, the second is present
the first is singular, the second plural
les-08.explain: 3PL:M has no prefix but does have the suffix -en. 2PL:M has prefix ṯ- and suffix -em. So the ṯ- prefix is ​​the signal for 'you' versus 'he/she'.

les-08.q: How do you say they sit (M / mixed, stem qqim)?
les-08.explain: STEM + -en, no prefix. A group of mixed men and women falls under the same masculine form.

les-08.q: Conjugate qqim for they sit — women only:
les-08.explain: STEM + -enṯ. This is the same ending as 2PL:V (ṯeqqimenṯ 'you V are sitting') — the difference is in the presence/absence of the prefix ṯ-.
n- + xḏem, with a schwa-e between n and x. The verb xḏem 'to work' (from Arabic) is used in all examples with aspect in Lesson 09.
n- = 1PL. No distinction between male and female in 'we' — just like in Dutch.
ṯ- + TRIBE + -enṯ is 2PL:V — a group in which all addressed are women. With a mixed group it would be ṯeqqimem.

les-08.q: Match each plural pattern to its person:
les-08.explain: With the four singular forms from Lesson 07 + these five you have the complete conjugation scheme. Nine forms — all other verbs follow the same pattern.

les-08.q: What is the imperative for you M in qqim?
les-08.explain: The imperative against one person is the bare stem (qqim 'sit!'). To you M / mixed: qqimeṯ or qqimem. To you Q: qqimenṯ.
3PL:M = STEM + -en: xḏemen. No prefix for the third person plural.
3PL:F = STEM + -enṯ: xḏemenṯ. The suffix -enṯ signals an exclusively female group.
2PL:M = ṯ- + STEM + -em: ṯexḏemem. The prefix ṯ- signals that it is "you" (not "they").

les-09.q: What does a Tarifit verb not directly encode?
options: whether the action has been completed
whether the promotion is still running
when the action took place (past / present / future)
les-09.explain: Tarifit encodes aspect, not time. You express time with particles (qa, ad, ṯuɣa) and context. For Dutch speakers, this is the biggest mental transition.

les-09.q: 'I've been working at that bakery for years' — which aspect form do you use?
les-09.explain: A habit or ongoing state → Imperfective. For 'work' it is xeddmeɣ. Only with qa before it (qa xeddmeɣ) does it become 'I'm working now'.

les-09.q: 'I ate bread yesterday' — which aspect form do you use?
les-09.explain: One completed event → Perfective. For 'eat' it is cciɣ 'I ate / I have eaten'. The Perfective covers both our present perfect ('ate') and imperfect ('at').

les-09.q: What does the particle qa do for a verb?
options: it makes the verb past tense
it turns it into a question
les-09.explain: qa + Imperfective = ongoing action now. Without qa the Imperfective has more of a habit meaning. qa is a pseudo-verb (Lesson 31).
teteɣ is the 1SG of the Imperfective of 'to eat' (root Imperfective: tett). With qa it becomes: 'currently busy eating'.
Perfective 1SG of 'eating' — completed action. The stem in the Perfective is cci (from Aorist cc + extra vowel). The translation can be 'I ate' or 'I ate'.

les-09.q: What is the Imperfective stem of cc 'food'?
les-09.explain: The Imperfective is completely different from the Aorist in many verbs. Here: cc → tett. That is why the course recommends: learn the three stems together for each verb — just like 'go / went / gone'.

les-09.q: What is the Imperfective stem of su 'to drink'?
les-09.explain: su → sess. Differs pattern-wise from cc → tett, although both are vowel-ending. Irregularity is the rule here.

les-09.q: Link each situation to the correct aspect form:

pairs.left: a habit ('he works as a baker')
what is happening now ('he is eating')

les-09.explain: Four core combinations — enough to accommodate 90% of what you hear in daily Tarifit. ad + Aorist you will discuss in Lesson 10.

les-09.q: Why is the Imperfective the most difficult part of Tarifit Conjugation?
options: it no longer exists in modern language
there are several patterns without a rule that is always correct — learning per verb
les-09.explain: Four main patterns (see explanation H4): doubling the second consonant, t-/tt- before it, changing the vowel, or combinations. No predictable rule — that's why you learn each verb with its three stems at the same time.

les-09.q: Which aspect do you use for an action that expresses a habit?
les-09.explain: A habit or ongoing state → Imperfective. You add the particle qa only when the action is happening right now.

les-09.q: What is the Imperfective stem of su "to drink"?
les-09.explain: The Imperfective stem of su "to drink" is sess. Just like cc → tett, you need to learn this stem form per verb.

les-09.q: What is the difference between cciɣ and qa teteɣ?
options: There is no difference in meaning
cciɣ = I have eaten (Perfective); qa teteɣ = I am eating (ongoing now)
cciɣ = I will eat; qa teteɣ = I have eaten
cciɣ is singular; qa teteɣ is plural
les-09.explain: cciɣ is the Perfective (completed action). qa teteɣ combines the particle qa with the Imperfective stem tett to express an ongoing action right now.

les-10.q: Which particle do you put in front of the Aorist to say 'I will eat'?
les-10.explain: ad marks that the action has not yet been completed. qa does just the opposite: being busy now (Lesson 09). ṯuɣa belongs to the past, ma introduces questions.

les-10.q: What follows after ad in this construction?
les-10.explain: ad + Aorist is the standard construction for future, wish or possibility. qa on the other hand, chooses the Imperfective.

les-10.q: Before a ṯ- or n- prefix, something happens with ad. What?
les-10.explain: ad ṯeffeɣ in practice becomes a ṯeffeɣ 'she will go out'. The same with a neffeɣ 'we will go outside'. A real Riffian writes it with a, not with ad.
Before 1SG (no ṯ- or n-), ad remains simply ad.

les-10.q: Complete: 'we will go outside' = ___ neffeɣ
les-10.explain: Before n-, ad merges into a. It literally once became ad neffeɣ, but you don't hear that anymore.
a = from ad; ṯeffeɣ = 3SG:V from ffeɣ 'to go outside'. ad sometimes also expresses wish or possibility, so 'she might go outside' is also conceivable in context.

accept: hij zou naar huis moeten gaan
les-10.explain: aggweḥ 'to go home' is its own verb (not a form of 'to go'). ad + Aorist here is future or wish, depending on the context.

les-10.q: xa yeyya instead of a yeyya — what is the speaker doing?
options: setting it in the distant future
express a stronger assumption — 'he will definitely come'
les-10.explain: xad (shortened to xa) is a modal variant of ad: more certainty, often with the connotation of a warning. Don't use it in subordinate clauses or after question words — it doesn't work there.

les-10.q: ad + Aorist always means future — true or false?
options: true — it is the default future
not true — it can also express wish, possibility or 'wanting'
les-10.explain: ad marks 'not-yet-realized' in a broad sense. Hence also xseɣ ad meřceɣ 'I want to get married' (lit. 'I want I-will-get-married' — Lesson 21).

les-10.q: Link each preverbal particle to its function:
les-10.explain: Four preverbal particles together control most of Tarifit verb semantics. You will discuss waa in Lesson 20.

les-10.q: How do you say "he will go home"? (verb: aggweḥ)
les-10.explain: ad + Aorist 3SG:M: ad yaggweḥ. Before the prefix y-, ad stays unchanged — the ḏ only drops before ṯ- and n-.

les-10.q: ad does not only express future. What can it also mean?
les-10.explain: ad marks "not yet realised" in a broad sense: future, wish, and possibility. Ongoing action right now is expressed with qa + Imperfective.

les-10.q: How do you say "she will go outside"? (verb: ffeɣ)
les-10.explain: Before the prefix ṯ-, ad is shortened to a: a ṯeffeɣ. The ḏ drops before ṯ- and n-.

les-11.q: What does the most feminine singular form look like?
les-11.explain: The golden rule: feminine = masculine surrounded by ṯ- on both sides. afunas 'beef' → ṯafunasṯ 'cow'.
āryaz 'man' begins with a- and ends in a consonant — typically masculine. The feminine counterpart here is not the regular variant but the suppletive ṯamɣārṯ 'woman'.
Standard derivation: ṯ- before, -ṯ after. Works like this for aɛabib → ṯaɛabibṯ, aḥenjia → ṯaḥenjiaṯ, etc.
ṯ- + afunas + -ṯ = ṯafunasṯ 'cow'. The a- remains in place.
ṯamɣārṯ 'woman' is not a regular derivation of āryaz 'man' — it is a separate root (suppletive). Just like 'cow' is not a derivative of 'bull' in Dutch.

les-11.q: Which pair does not follow the regular ṯ-…-ṯ rule?
les-11.explain: āryaz and ṯamɣārṯ have completely different roots — typically suppletive. Like amyan / ṯyatṯ 'goat/goat', yis / řeɛawḏa 'horse/mare'.

les-11.q: What is the gender of languages in Tarifit?
les-11.explain: Languages ​​are feminine by default: ṯmazixṯ 'Berber language', ṯaɛrabṯ 'Arabic', ṯaspanyuṯ 'Spanish'. The same word also means 'a woman from that language community'.
Here the feminine form serves as a diminutive: akeccuḏ = 'big stick', ṯakeccutṯ = 'twig'. The same pattern with attaw 'big eye' / ṯitṯ 'plain eye'.
Important insight: not every M-word has a regular V-pendant. For people/animals where the two really differ, Tarifit uses separate stems — just like Dutch.

les-12.q: The main rule for masculine plural: a- becomes...
les-12.explain: afunas 'bovine' → ifunasen 'cattle'. Often there is also a -en or -an behind the trunk.

les-12.q: The main rule for feminine plural: ṯa- becomes … and …
les-12.explain: ṯafunasṯ 'cow' → ṯifunasin 'cows'. Vowel shift in front (ṯa- → ṯi-) and a suffix -in in the back.
a- becomes i-, and after the stem becomes -en. The main pattern.
ṯa- → ṯi-, suffix -in. Note: in the plural the -ṯ disappears at the end.
Singular is azru 'stone'. Here the root vowel also changes: u becomes a. Pattern that you have to learn word by word.
Singular is aydi 'dog'. Completely different root — a suppletive plural, comparable to Dutch 'person / people'.

les-12.q: What is special about uř → uřawen 'heart / hearts'?
options: an element -aw- is inserted between stem and suffix
the plural is identical to singular
les-12.explain: -aw--infix occurs in monosyllabic stems: uř → uřawen, ṯitṯ → ṯitṯawin 'eye / eyes'.

options: a plural without an ending letter
a plural with a completely different root than the singular
a plural that only occurs in literature
les-12.explain: Examples: uma → ayeṯma 'brother/brothers', aydi → iṯan 'dog/dogs'. No distractions — just learning as a couple.

les-12.q: Match the plural pattern to the type:

pairs.right: main rule V: ṯa- → ṯi- + -in

les-12.explain: Five main patterns. Practical advice from the course: always learn singular + plural together — just like German 'der Mann / die Männer'.

les-12.q: Someone says 'I have 1 sheep, but for 2 I would never guess what the plural is'. What's the best advice?
options: no problem — there is one predictable rule
no big deal — there are no plurals in Tarifit
learn singular + plural per word as a pair — there is no rule that is always correct
les-12.explain: In addition to the main rule, there are stem shifts, infix -aw- and suppletive plurals. No prediction rule works 100% — hence: pairwise learning.

les-13.q: What does baba mean by itself, without further addition?
options: my father - the property '1SG' is already built in
a formal address for older men
les-13.explain: Family words in Tarifit have already processed 'my': baba = 'my father', yemma = 'my mother', mmi = 'my son'. For someone else's father you say baba-c, baba-s etc.

les-13.q: What suffix do you use on a family word for 'your' (M)?
les-13.explain: -c = 2SG:M ('your' vs man). Against queen: -m. -s is 3SG (his/hers), -neɣ is 1PL ('our').
yemma = 'my mother'. With suffix -c: 'your mother' (M).
uma = 'my brother'. Suffix -s = 3SG (his/her). The same -s covers both 'his' and 'her'.

options: also direct suffixes such as -c, -s
the preposition n + possessive form (inu, nnec, nnes…)
les-13.explain: Two systems side by side: family words attach the property directly, all other words use a separate property form after n: ṯaḏḏarṯ-inu 'my house', ṯaḏḏarṯ nnec 'your house (M)'.
Literally 'the house of mine'. inu is the special 1SG holding form — irregular: not nni as the pattern would predict.

nnes = 'his/hers' — gender difference does not exist here. Context determines whether it is 'his' or 'her'. āryaz-nnes could therefore also be 'his husband' — although this is more unlikely in a traditional context.

options: it is no longer used by young people
it is the only possession form at n that does not start with nn-
it only exists in formal language
les-13.explain: The pattern nn- + suffix works for all other persons (nnec, nnem, nnes, nneɣ, nwem…). Only 1SG breaks it: inu, not *nni.
Non-family word → two words: independent nw + possession. Against woman it would be ṯaḏḏarṯ nnem.

les-13.q: Match each possession to its meaning:
les-13.explain: Remember: 'you' always splits into M (-c) and V (-m); 'him' and 'her' coincide in -s.

les-14.q: What suffix does 'this' mean (close to the speaker)?
les-14.explain: -a = close (this). -in = further away or near the listener(s). -enni = already mentioned in the conversation.

les-14.q: What does -enni express that Dutch does not have so distinctly?
options: 'which we already mentioned in this conversation' — a kind of 'aforementioned'
les-14.explain: Three degrees of distance: spatial (-a, -in) plus 'discursive' (-enni 'earlier in this conversation'). English 'aforementioned X' comes closest.

les-14.q: How do you write this man (āryaz + 'this')?
les-14.explain: Suffix -a immediately after the noun. Written with a dash or solid, you can see both. The spelling with a dash makes the morphology visible.

les-14.q: How do you write that man (āryaz + 'that one, further away')?
les-14.explain: Suffix -in. The same pattern works for V (ṯaḏḏarṯ-in 'that house') and MV (irgazen-in 'those men').

accept: die man waar we het over hadden
les-14.explain: Literally 'that man we mentioned earlier'. Indispensable in stories - this is how you signal that a character is already known to the listener.

les-14.q: What is wa (without suffix) when it stands alone?
options: loose demonstrative pronoun 'this' (M, ev) — without noun
les-14.explain: Individual pointers are without a noun: wa 'this (M)', ṯa 'this (V)', ina 'this (M-MV)', ṯina 'this (V-MV)'. The 'this one you hold' = wa.
ḏa = here; ḏin = there; ḏiha = over there, far away. Three distances — just like the pointers.

les-14.q: What is the difference between ḏin and ḏiha?
options: ḏin = there (visible / closer); ḏiha = over there (far, often out of sight)
ḏin is M, ḏiha is V
ḏin is past, ḏiha is future
les-14.explain: Tarifit distinguishes two levels of 'there'. ḏiha marks true distance or non-visibility — similar to Spanish 'allí' vs 'allá'.
řexxu 'now' is a common adverb. Often occurs in dialogues: řexxu ḏ necc 'now it's me'.

les-14.q: Match each separate demonstrative pronoun with its meaning:
les-14.explain: Three distances × two genders × ev/mv = twelve forms in total. All follow w-/ṯ-/i-/ṯi- + a/in/enni.

options: a form that only occurs after a preposition
the dictionary form — the word 'at rest', alone or at the beginning of the sentence
les-15.explain: The free state (FS) is what you find in a glossary. āryaz 'man', ṯafunasṯ 'cow' — these are FS forms.

les-15.q: When do you use the connected state?
options: especially after prepositions and as a subject after the verb
les-15.explain: Connected state (AS) appears where the noun attaches to something: after most prepositions (n wāryaz 'of the man') and as a VSO subject (yexḏem wāryaz 'the man works').

les-15.q: What happens to a- when transitioning to connected state (M ev)?
les-15.explain: āryaz (FS) → wāryaz (AS); afunas → wafunas. The w- points to the old emphasis that was lost in FS.
For example in yeqqim wāryaz 'the man stayed' (subject after verb, so AS).
V ev: ṯa- becomes ṯ-. The a disappears. Ditto ṯamɣārṯ → ṯmɣārṯ.
The verb comes first (VSO), the subject āryaz comes after and therefore must be in AS — hence wāryaz. Sentence order is elaborated in Lesson 16.

les-15.q: What is the difference between āryaz yexḏem and yexḏem wāryaz?
options: the first is past, the second is present
the first is a question, the second a statement
no difference in meaning - only position and therefore: SV (FS) or VS (AS)
the first is M, the second V
les-15.explain: Both mean 'the man works'. The difference is in structure: subject in front = FS (āryaz); subject after ww = AS (wāryaz). Stylistically and emphatically different, but not semantically.

les-15.q: What type of word has no state distinction?
options: Class II loanwords (ssaḇun 'soap') and family words (baba)
les-15.explain: Class II (Arabic loanwords) and Class III (family words) remain unchanged in any position. Adjectives are also always in the free state — regardless of the word they describe.

les-15.q: After which two prepositions do you use — exceptionally — the free condition?
options: none — all prepositions take a connected state
les-15.explain: břa āryaz-nnes 'without her husband' — a preposition, but FS. Almost all other prepositions trigger AS. This is worth a mnemonic.

les-15.q: Which state corresponds to the position?
les-15.explain: Mnemonic: 'at rest' = FS, 'in a group' (attached to verb or preposition) = AS. Once automatic, you can read the difference immediately.

les-16.explain: V = Verb (verb), S = Subject, O = Object. In Tarifit the standard order is: verb first, then the subject. Dutch is usually SVO or SOV.

les-16.q: What state is the subject in when it comes after the verb?
les-16.explain: After the verb (VSO order): connected state. yexḏem wāryaz — wāryaz (AS) because the subject is after the ww. Lesson 15 covered this as a principle; here you see it in action.

accept: de man is aan het werken
les-16.explain: Literally 'the man works' — VSO. But Dutch puts the subject first, so you translate it as 'the man works'.

les-16.q: You want to say 'the man works' with emphasis on 'the man'. How do you do that?
options: āryaz, yexḏem — subject first (topicalization, free state)
that is not possible in Tarifit
les-16.explain: Topicalization: the subject in front in the free state, a comma after it, then the verb. This way you emphasize 'the man' (and not someone else). It is grammatical, but deviates from the usual order.

les-16.q: Is it mandatory to pronounce the subject in a Tarifit sentence?
options: no — the verb conjugation already says who does it
les-16.explain: Pro-drop: yexḏem means 'he works' — no need for a separate 'he'. The prefix y- already marks 3SG:M. Same as in Spanish or Arabic.

les-16.q: Translation: qa yewca baba ṯṯmenyaṯ i Mimun
les-16.correct: mijn vader heeft geld aan Mimoun gegeven
accept: mijn vader heeft geld aan Mimoun gegeven
mijn vader gaf geld aan Mimoun
les-16.explain: Order: qa (aspect) — yewca (verb) — baba (subject, family word = no state change) — ṯṯmenyaṯ (object) — i Mimun (prepositional phrase). Classical VSO + prepositional phrase at the back.

les-16.q: What is the function of qa in qa yewca baba ṯṯmenyaṯ i Mimun?
options: it is the verb for 'to give'
it marks that the action is ongoing or has already taken place (aspect particle)
les-16.explain: qa is preverbal and indicates that the action is reality — in progress or has already happened. See Lesson 09 for the aspect operation of qa.

les-16.q: Match each sequence with its meaning or function:
les-16.explain: VSO is the basic rule, but Tarifit is more flexible than you think: clitics, topicalization and question constructions can adjust the order.

les-17.q: Which two prepositions take free state instead of connected state?
les-17.explain: aṛ and břa are the two exceptions. All other prepositions trigger connected state.
ḏi ṯaḏḏarṯ 'in the house'. Triggers connected state.
x uyis 'on the horse'. Associated state of ayis is uyis.
zi = 'of, from'. Geographic names do not change state (Class II).

les-17.q: What is the difference between s and akeḏ?
les-17.explain: s ṯmazixṯ 'in Berber' (middle); akeḏ uma-s 'with his brother' (together). Just like Dutch 'with a hammer' vs 'with my friend'.

les-17.q: Tarifit has no verb for 'to have'. How do you express 'I have a car'?
options: ɣari ijjen ṯṯumubin (one car with me)
les-17.explain: ɣaa + person = 'at X'. ɣari = ɣaa + -i (for me). Literally 'one car with me' = 'I have a car'.

les-17.q: How do you say 'with him' (possession construction)?
les-17.explain: ɣaa + suffix -s (3SG) = ɣaas. Example: ɣaas ijj uma-s 'she has a brother'.
břa takes free state — hence ṯamɣārṯ (FS). nnes = 'his/her'.

les-17.q: Match each preposition to its meaning:
les-17.explain: Note: ḏ as 'and' only works between noun phrases.
ɣaaneɣ = ɣaa + -neɣ (with us). Literally 'with us a house' = 'we have a house'.

les-18.q: What is the only Berber (non-Arabic) number from 1 to 10?
les-18.explain: ijjen / icṯen is Berber heritage. The rest (2–10) are loanwords from Arabic — useful if you know Arabic.

les-18.q: Why does 'one' have two forms (ijjen and icṯen)?
options: ijjen is masculine, icṯen is feminine
the first is formal, the second informal
les-18.explain: Only '1' makes a gender distinction: ijjen wāryaz 'a man', icṯ ṯamɣārṯ 'a woman'. Numbers 2–10 have no gender forms.
ṯřaṯa is the Tarifit pronunciation of the Arabic thalatha (three). Note the ř — in Tarifit the old l has become a ř sound.
seḇɛa — from Arabic sab'a. The ɛ is the Arabic 'ayn sound.
For 2 and higher there is always n 'van' between the number and the noun: number + n + noun (pl). Literally 'three of women'.
With 'one' you use no n. ijjen wāryaz — right next to each other, the noun in a connected state (wāryaz).
Like German ein or English one/a: ijjen ṯaḏḏarṯ can mean 'a house' or 'one house'. Context determines whether it is a numeral or an article.
ɛecra — from Arabic 'ashara. The ɛ is the 'ayn sound.
You already know the 'odd' numbers 3, 5, 7 (ṯřaṯa, xemsa, seḇɛa). Learn 2, 4, 6, 8, 9 as a new set.
xemsa (5) + n + yewdan (plural of 'person'). Standard pattern.

les-19.explain: wi yewṯa uḥenjia-nni? 'Who hit the boy?' The question word comes first — the verb normally follows afterwards.
meřmi ṯṯettsed? 'When do you sleep?' Note the ř — not a regular r.
mayemmi ṯeṯrud? 'Why are you crying?' mayemmi = literally something like 'what causes?'.
mamec yegga manay-a? 'How did he do that?' mamec asks about the way.

les-19.q: Which particle opens a formal yes/no question?
les-19.explain: ma ḏ cekk? 'Is it you?' — ma at the beginning makes it an explicit question. You can also just increase the intonation, just like in Dutch.

les-19.q: What is the difference between mani and manis?
options: mani asks about people, manis about places
les-19.explain: mani ṯṯiřid? 'Where do you live?' versus manis ɣa ṯaḏfeḏ? 'What are you going into?' (which side / from which direction).
mecḥař iwezzen? 'How much does it weigh?' Comes from Arabic shḥal.
Preposition zi 'from/from' + question word meřmi 'when' = 'from when / since when'. Prepositions combine freely with question words.
Eight question words in total in the lesson. The five here are the most frequent. meřmi (when) and mayemmi (why) are extra.

les-20.q: How do you wrap a verb to say 'not'?
les-20.explain: Just like French ne... pas: waa comes before it, ca comes after it. Both are necessary in standard negation.
yus-d 'hij is gekomen' → waa yus-d ca 'hij is niet gekomen'. Note: the verb form itself can also change in negation (see Negative Perfective).

les-20.q: When negating the Perfective, the verb form changes. What is changing?
options: nothing at all — denial is always the same
the a in the stem becomes i (Negative Perfective)
les-20.explain: Example: wda (fall, Pf.) → wdi (NP): waa wdi ca 'he did not fall'. Same: řmeḏ → řmiḏ, udef → udif.
Prohibition: waa + Imperfective (no ca). tett is the Imperfective of 'eat'. Compare: waa ṯeggweḏ ca 'do not be afraid' — also Imperfective, but here with optional ca.

les-20.q: How do you deny 'I ate' (cciɣ)?
les-20.explain: waa + cciɣ + ca. The stem cc does not change here (no a to change to i).
waa … ḥedd = 'nobody'. Literally 'no one saw him'. The denier ḥedd replaces the subject.
ɛemmaas waa d-yusi 'he never came'. walu = 'nothing', ḥedd = 'nobody', ura ḏ = 'not even'.

les-20.q: Translate: cem waaǧi bu ḏ yemma
les-20.explain: waaǧi denies a noun predicate ('X is not Y'). Different from waa + verb: that negates verb phrases.
Five denial patterns. Remember: waa … ca is the basic version. The rest are specializations for specific negation meanings.

les-20.q: How do you deny 'he will eat' (ad yecc)?
options: waa yetett ca — Negative Imperfective without ad
les-20.explain: When negating ad + Aorist, use the Negative Imperfective without ad. So don't waa ad yecc — that's incorrect.

les-21.q: In Dutch, after 'I want' there is an infinitive: 'I want to go'. What does Tarifit use?
options: two fully conjugated verbs next to each other
only the Perfective of the second verb
les-21.explain: xseɣ ad meřceɣ = literally 'I-want-I-will-get-married'. Both verbs are conjugated for the same person. Tarifit has no infinitive — this is the standard substitution.
xseɣ ad ariɣ 'I want to write'. The particle ad marks the unrealized action — the same function as in future constructions (Lesson 10). The same applies to zemmaa 'be able to'.
yebda yeṯxemmem 'he began to think' — yeṯxemmem is the Imperfective of 'think'. Same with qqim 'continue with': always Imperfective.
xseɣ = 1SG of xes 'want'. ad ariɣ = 1SG Aorist of ari 'write' with future particle.
zemmaa 'can', negated: waa zemmaay ca. sba = wait. ad sbaay = 'I will wait'. Together: 'I can't wait'.
zemmaa + ad + Aorist. Just like xes: both take ad + Aorist as complement.

les-21.q: How do you express 'he became a doctor'?
les-21.explain: dweř = 'become' (change of state). ḏ + noun express the new state. qa yedweř ḏ adbib = 'he became a doctor'.

les-21.q: How do you say 'he knows that I will write'?
les-21.explain: illa introduces a 'that' clause after verbs such as 'know', 'say', 'see'. In negation: ma instead of illa.

les-21.q: Link auxiliary verb to its complement:
les-21.explain: Two groups: 'want/can' takes ad + Aorist; 'begin/continue' takes Imperfective. dweř is the exception.

les-22.q: Which suffix is ​​the direct object 'him / her / it' after the verb?
les-22.explain: -ṯ = 3SG DO (him/her/it). yecc-iṯ 'he ate it'. The i before the suffix is ​​a connecting vowel that appears after a vowel-ending verb.

les-22.q: What is the difference between DO suffix -ṯ and IO suffix -as?
options: -ṯ = direct object (him/her); -as = indirect object (to him/her)
les-22.explain: yecc-iṯ 'he ate it' (DO). yenna-as 'he said to him/her' (IO). Two separate suffix sets — similar to Dutch 'hem' (acc.) vs 'aan hem' (dat.).

les-22.correct: hij heeft hem naar buiten gelaten
accept: hij heeft hem naar buiten gelaten
les-22.explain: ssufeɣ 'to let out' (causative of ffeɣ) + -iṯ (DO him/her). The i is a connecting vowel between vowel stem and clitic.
ṯenna-ayi 'she said to me'. DO suffix 'me' is also -ayi — both coincide for 1SG. Meaning depends on the verb.
wciɣ-as pabu 'I gave him a turkey'. -as is the IO of 3SG — gender not expressed.
-am = IO 2SG:V (to you, woman). Against man it would be yenna-ac.

les-22.q: What is the fixed order if you attach both IO and DO to the verb?
les-22.explain: yiwy-ac-ṯ-id 'he brought it hither for you': -ac (IO to you) — -ṯ (DO it) — -iḏ (hither). Always in that order.

les-22.q: What does the suffix -d (hither) do to a verb?
options: it makes the verb past tense
it indicates that the action is towards the speaker
it turns it into a question
les-22.explain: yedweř ɣaa Naḍuār (speaker not in Nador) vs yedweř-d ɣaa Naḍuār (speaker is in Nador). The speaker's perspective is ingrained in the verb.
DO suffixes are more compact than free pronouns. Learn them as a set: -ayi / -c / -cem / -ṯ / -aneɣ / …

les-23.q: How do you connect two nouns with 'and'?
options: not a separate word — just next to each other
les-23.explain: necc ḏ uma 'me and my brother'. ḏ only works between noun phrases. You connect two verb phrases by simply placing them next to each other (juxtaposition).

les-23.q: How do you connect two verb phrases with 'and'?
les-23.explain: Tarifit simply juxtaposes sentences: 'he did this, he did that'. The distinction with ḏ is subtle but grammatically correct — ḏ really only belongs to nouns.
ma ḏ azeggwaɣ niɣ ḏ acemřař? 'Is it red or white?' niɣ works both between NPs and between sentences.

les-23.q: What is the nuance difference between maca and seɛɛa?
options: maca = plain 'but'; seɛɛa = 'but in reality / actually'
les-23.explain: seɛɛa expresses a correction or contrast: 'I thought X, but in reality it is Y'. maca is the neutral opposite.

les-23.q: What 'if' do you use for an open hypothesis ('if you want...')?
les-23.explain: mařa ṯexseḏ a ḏam-ṯ-newc 'if you want, we will give it to you' — an open condition that can come true. mři / meɛlik are counterfactual: the situation is not the case.

les-23.correct: als ik gekomen was, zou ik gegeten hebben
accept: als ik gekomen was zou ik gegeten hebben
als ik was gekomen had ik gegeten
les-23.explain: Counterfactual: I didn't come, so I didn't eat either. mři triggers clitic-fronting in the subordinate clause (see also Lesson 10 explanation).

les-23.q: When do you use umi and when xmi?
options: umi is past, xmi is question word
les-23.explain: umi ḏ-yusa 'when he came here' (past). xmi ɣa ṯaḏfeḏ 'when you enter' (future/present). Similar to the difference between English when (past) and when (future) in subordinate clauses.
Both puřki and lianna are common. lianna is more Arabic-oriented. puřki feels more Tarifit-specific.
Five basic conjunctions. Combine them with tense markers (umi, xmi, awaṛn umi) to build complex sentences.

les-24.q: What does tuɣa do in a sentence?
options: it puts the situation in the past — 'was / was busy'
les-24.explain: tuɣa-c ḏ ameddukeř inu 'you were my friend'. tuɣa is not a verb but a particle that places the situation before now. Negative: tuyi.
tuɣa + suffix -ayi (me) = 'I was'. ḏi ṯaḏḏarṯ = 'in the house'. Together: 'I was home'.
ṯiwecca — remember the initial ṯ (feminine prefix). Occurs frequently in stories describing 'the next morning'.
řebda = always, always. Note the ř (not a regular r — see Lesson 25).

les-24.q: Why does 'two years' have a separate form (ɛamayen) instead of '2 + n + years'?
options: that is the Arabic dualise — a special dual ending
it is an exception without reason
it is the same as three years
les-24.explain: Arabic has a dualis ending -ayen for two units. Tarifit has adopted them for day, month and year: yumayen (two days), cehrayen (two months), ɛamayen (two years).
ṯeřṯ snin — here the Arabic plural snin is used (years). For 3+, use the normal counting structure but with snin, not ɛam.

les-24.q: Translation: zzman tuɣa ṯnayen n duru tsekkʷa
les-24.correct: vroeger was twee duro veel waard
accept: vroeger was twee duro veel waard
in de oude tijd was twee duro veel waard
les-24.explain: zzman = 'back in the day, in the old days'. tuɣa = 'was'. ṯnayen n duro = 'two duro'. tsekkʷa = 'has value'. Classic use of zzman + tuɣa together.

les-24.q: How do you say 'during the day'?
les-24.explain: s = with / in (instrument preposition). nnhaa = day. Literally 'by the day'. Same pattern: s ǧiřeṯ = 'at night'.

pairs.right: back in the day, in the old days

les-24.explain: Five core temporal adverbs. Combine them with tuɣa (was) or the verb aspect forms to situate temporal contexts.

les-25.q: Tarifit has three R letters. Which historically comes from a l?
les-25.explain: In other Berber dialects it is still simply l. In Nador-Tarifit it has been changed to ř. Hence uř (heart) where other dialects have ul.

les-25.q: What did double ll change to Nador-Tarifit?
les-25.explain: yelli (daughter in other dialects) → yeǧi. ulli (cattle) → uǧi. The double ll is a softer variant than single l, and coincided with the ǧ sound.
taɣyult (donkey in other dialects) → ṯaɣyutc. The combination l+t assimilated to tc. You also see this in the 'egg' example from the lesson: ṯameǧatc.

les-25.q: How do we write Naḍur in the learntarifit alphabet (vocalized r)?
les-25.explain: -ur → notation -uār (macron above a, r remains). Hence Naḍuār. Sounds like 'Naadoer': the r has become vocal.

les-25.q: What happens to -ar at the end of a word through vocalization?
options: becomes -ār (macron above a, r remains in spelling; sounds like long a)
les-25.explain: Pattern: -ar → spelling -ār. aayaz → āryaz 'man'. The r remains in spelling but sounds like a long a.

les-25.q: What happens to -ir through vocalization?
les-25.explain: Pattern: -ir → spelling -yār. irden (wheat) → yārḏen. Sounds like yaaḏen: the i + r becomes a long yaa.

les-25.q: When does no vocalization of the r occur?
options: if the r is followed by a real vowel (a, i, u)
if the word has more than two syllables
les-25.explain: ru 'cry' — r before u → regular r. ari 'write' — r before i → regular r. Vocalization only occurs where the r is not immediately followed by a vowel.

les-25.q: Link the parent language pattern to the Nador-Tarifit variant:
les-25.explain: Four sound laws in one lesson. Together they explain why many Tarifit words look different from related Berber languages ​​— but the structure is the same.

les-25.q: A speaker says ṯamɣārṯ. Which written word belongs to this?
les-25.explain: Vocalization pattern: -ar → spelling -ār. So ṯamɣārṯ 'woman'. The pronunciation sounds like ṯamɣārṯ. Also on this site as ṯamɣārṯ.

les-26.q: Adjectives in Tarifit behave grammatically like…
options: nouns — they inflect for gender and number
les-26.explain: ameqqṛan (large, M:SG) → ṯameqqṛanṯ (F:SG) → imeqqṛanen (M:PL). Like nouns: a-/ṯa--prefix, -ṯ-suffix for V, i-…-en for M:PL.

les-26.q: Give the feminine singular form of amezzyan 'small':
les-26.explain: Standard pattern: ṯa- + stem + -ṯ. Same as with nouns in lesson 11.

les-26.q: Give the masculine plural form of azeggʷaɣ 'red':
les-26.explain: a- → i-, suffix -en. Standard plural pattern.

les-26.q: How do you say 'the big country' (specific)?
les-26.explain: Particular noun phrase: noun + adjective directly next to each other, without ḏ. ḏ is only used with indefinite: ijjen weyyur ḏ ameqqṛan 'a big donkey'.

les-26.q: How do you say 'a big house' (indefinite)?
les-26.explain: Indefinite: ijjen (one) + noun + ḏ + e.g. nv. The ḏ acts as a linking element here. Compare: definite = next to each other, indefinite = with ḏ.

les-26.q: You write n wāryaz ameqqṛan 'of the great man'. What state is ameqqṛan in?
options: connected — because it is after n
free state — adjectives always remain free
les-26.explain: Adjectives are always in a free state, regardless of the state of the noun before it. wāryaz is AS (after n), but ameqqṛan remains FS.

les-26.q: Which two adjectives do not inflect for gender or number?
les-26.explain: jjdid 'new' and nneɣni 'other' are invariant — they were borrowed from Arabic and never adopted the Berber inflection pattern.
Literally 'the car that is expensive'. Many 'adjectival' qualities are expressed in Tarifit through a relative clause (Lesson 32). yeyran = 'he is expensive' (Perfective of 'to be expensive').

les-26.q: Match each adjective with its meaning:
les-26.explain: Colors and properties. azegza covers both blue and green — as in many other languages, there is one word for the bluish-green spectrum.

les-27.q: What does the collective form such as ɛenba mean?
options: the species in general — grapes as a category
les-27.explain: sɣiɣ ɛenba 'I bought grapes' — not one specific grape, but grapes as a mass or species. You use this for 'do you have apples?', 'I like to eat figs', etc.

les-27.q: How do you make the collective ɛenba the countable singular 'one grape'?
options: not a separate word — context determines it
les-27.explain: Countable singular = feminine singular (with ṯa-…-ṯ). This is a systematic rule: ɛenba → ṯaɛenbaṯ; řbacua → ṯbacuaṯ.

les-27.q: How do you say 'I bought grapes' (the kind, not one piece)?
les-27.explain: Collective ɛenba — no feminine prefix or suffix needed. Just like English 'I bought grapes' without article.

les-27.q: How do you say 'I ate one fig'?
les-27.explain: ṯbacuaṯ = one fig (countable V-ev). The collective was řbacua (figs in general).
Countable plural = feminine plural (ṯi-…-in). Three or more pieces: numeral + n + V-pl. ṯiɛenbaṯin = grapes (counting).

options: it exists only as a plural (plural tantum) — also for one mass
les-27.explain: aman is always grammatically plural, even when you are talking about one glass of water. Just like Dutch 'shears' (always mv) or Arabic miyaah. řehrua (herbs) also falls into this category.
řbacua = collective (figs as a species). qa attas = 'there are many'. Collectively used as the subject of a general statement.

les-27.q: Match usage with the correct form for 'řbacua' (figs):
les-27.explain: Three layers: collective (kind) → countable singular (one piece, V:SG) → countable plural (pieces, V:PL). A system that you also encounter in Arabic.

les-28.q: What does the prefix aṯ mean in aṯ Naḍuār?
les-28.explain: aṯ Naḍuār = 'those of Nador' (the people of Nador). Also used for tribal affiliation: aṯ Iqeṛɛiyen = 'the Iqeṛɛiyen tribe'.

les-28.q: What does the prefix bu- express?
les-28.explain: bu ṯmarṯ = 'the one with the beard'. bu ṯɣanjayṯ = 'the one with the spoon' (the cook). bu- creates nicknames based on a prominent feature.
bu + ṯmarṯ (beard). In Riffian culture, this is a common, non-negative nickname. Someone can be known like that all their life.

les-28.q: What is the feminine variant of bu-?
les-28.explain: mm ṯaḥcunṯ = 'the one with the nice ass'. The prefix mm- / m- is the feminine counterpart of bu-.

les-28.q: What does the prefix u- mean in old names such as u-Mmuh?
les-28.explain: u-Mmuh = 'Mmuh's son'. This u- can be found in many old Berber names and place names. It is related to the Arabic ibn 'son of'.

les-28.q: What do you call a woman/man 'that of Nador' in the plural (members of Nador)?
les-28.explain: aṯ Naḍuār is already a plural-like construction — it refers to the group of people from Nador. For the individual: 'a Nadorling' would be described differently.

les-28.q: What is the plural of arifi 'Riffijn'?
les-28.explain: Plurals of root membership words: a- → i-, suffix -yen. arifi → irifiyen. Same pattern: aspanyu → ispunya, aliman → ilimanen.
Four prefixes to name people based on origin or characteristic. bu- nicknames are culturally common in the Rif.

les-29.q: What does the prefix ss- on a verb mean?
options: it places the action in the past
les-29.explain: Causative: cc 'to eat' → ssecc 'to feed/feed'. Dutch uses two separate verbs; Tarifit does the same with one prefix.
ss- + cc = ssecc 'to feed, to feed'. Note: the stem is already a double consonant, which remains.
ssřmeḏ = 'to teach'. Default: ss- + stem. No sound change needed here.

les-29.q: Rule 1: a verb with double initial consonant (such as ggenfa) — what happens to the causative case?
options: the prefix becomes s- instead of ss-
les-29.explain: ggenfa → sgenfa (not ssggenfa). The double initial vowel becomes single to prevent stacking. Likewise bbdu → sbedu.

les-29.q: How does ffeɣ become 'going out' as a causative?
les-29.explain: Rule 2: verbs with a double initial consonant and only one subsequent consonant get a u between prefix and stem: ss + u + feɣ = ssufeɣ 'let out'.

les-29.q: How does adef become 'to enter' as a causative?
les-29.explain: Rule 3: Verbs with initial a — which a becomes i: ssidef. Same: aheř → ssiheř 'to tire'.
sgenfa = causative of ggenfa 'to heal (to get better yourself)'. With ss- it becomes 'making it heal'. -yi = me (DO suffix).

accept: hij geeft zijn hond te eten
les-29.explain: ssecc = causative of cc 'food'. aydi-nnes = 'his dog' (related state of aydi).

les-29.q: Link basic verb to causative case:
les-29.explain: One prefix, dozens of new verbs. Once you master the three sound rules, you can build each causative yourself.

les-30.q: What does mm- (or its variants) primarily express?
options: a reciprocal or middle meaning — 'Xing each other'
les-30.explain: neɣ 'kill' → mneɣ 'fight' (= kill each other). řaɣa 'call' → mřaɣa 'call each other'. It is not the same as reflexive ('itself') — that goes via ixef-nnes.
řaɣa 'call' + reflexive prefix mř- = mřaɣa. The variant mř- appears for stems with an initial a.

les-30.q: What is the difference between mm- (reciprocal) and ixef-nnes?
options: mm- is past; ixef-nnes is the future
mm- is formal; ixef-nnes is informal
les-30.explain: Pitfall for Dutch speakers: mm- is neither reflexive nor identical to 'itself'. yewṯa ixef-nnes = 'he hit himself'. mneɣ = 'they kill each other'.

les-30.q: What does twa- do on a verb?
options: makes a real passive — 'X is done'
les-30.explain: zzu 'to plant' → twazzu 'to be planted'. cc 'to eat' → twacc 'to be eaten'. Difference with mm-: twa- is always passive without an actor.

les-30.q: What are the two limitations of twa-?
options: you cannot name the actor, and there is no imperfective form
les-30.explain: Important: twacc = 'it was eaten', but you CANNOT say 'it was eaten by John'. Furthermore, twa- has no Imperfective — only Perfective.
menz 'to sell', mm- variant → temmenz 'to be sold' (Perfect). ṯṯumubin-nni = 'that car' (-nni = aforementioned).

les-30.q: What does it mean when tetmenza ṯṯumubin-nni is in the Imperfective?
options: “that car is sellable” — possibility, not outcome
it can't be — twa- has no Imperfective
les-30.explain: This is a subtle point from the explanation: with mm- verbs (not with twa-) the Imperfective form sometimes has a 'can become X' meaning. tetmenza = 'she is salable'.

les-30.q: Combine prefixes: passive from ssizzeř 'let run' — what is the result?
les-30.explain: twa- + sizzeř = twasizzeř 'to be made to run'. Prefixes can be stacked: causative → then passive over it.
Three productive verb prefixes + the reflexive construction. Together they are the entire system of Tarifit verb derivation.

les-31.q: What makes a pseudo-verb different from a regular verb?
options: it does not have aspect triplets (Perfective / Imperfective / Aorist), but can receive personal suffixes
it only exists in the plural
it is never used in everyday speech
les-31.explain: Pseudo-verbs behave at the interface: they do take pronoun suffixes and the direction element -d, but have no verb aspect. Compare French voici: not a verb, but you can say le-voici.

options: it presents something or someone — 'look here, here is...'
les-31.explain: aqqa ṯxaḏenṯ 'here is the ring'. aqq-eṯ 'here he is'. aqq-ayi 'here I am'. The stem aqq- then takes the DO suffix.
The standard greeting in Tarifit. Literally: 'are you looking — well?' aqq-ec = 'you here' (2SG suffix). mliḥ = 'good'. Already learned in Lesson 05 — now you see the pseudo-verb structure.

les-31.q: How do you say 'here I am' with aqqa?
les-31.explain: aqq- + DO suffix -ayi (me) = aqq-ayi. You don't have to add a separate pronoun.

accept: ik dacht dat het waar was
naar mijn idee is het waar
les-31.explain: ṯɣiř + IO suffix = 'it looks like X'. -ayi = to me. ḏ ssehh = 'it is the truth'. Together: 'it seems true to me'.

les-31.q: What are the three main uses of qa?
options: locative ('here is'), ongoing action (+ Imperfective), recent perfective ('just happened')
les-31.explain: qa-ṯ ḏiha (he is there). qa yetru (he is crying). qa yenna-ac (he just told you...). Three functions, one particle.

options: in subordinate clauses or after question words
les-31.explain: qa is a main clause particle. After question words (min, mani) and in subordinate clauses it is dropped and you use the verb form without qa. Nor can it be denied.
ṯuɣa + suffix -c (you) = 'you were'. ḏ ameddukeř inu = 'my friend'. Negative: ṯuyi.
Five pseudo-verbs, each with its own niche. qa and ṯuɣa are the most frequent in stories and conversations.

les-32.q: How does an indefinite relative clause work in Tarifit?
options: there is a separate 'that/that' as a connector
the subordinate clause sticks directly after the indefinite main word, with a pronoun that followed back
the verb takes on a participle form
les-32.explain: iwden ɣaa ijjen ṯaḏḏarṯ [ṯexřa] 'they came to a house that was deserted'. The subordinate clause comes immediately after ṯaḏḏarṯ, and ṯexřa refers back to the house (anaphoric pronoun).

les-32.q: What is a characteristic of the certain relative clause?
options: there is a referring pronoun in the subordinate clause
the verb in the subordinate clause sometimes gets a participle form (y-STAM-en), no referrer
it is always the same as the indefinite clause
les-32.explain: Determined: āryaz [d-yusin] 'the man who came here'. yusin is a participle-like form. No separate pronoun that refers back to 'the man'.

les-32.q: What does the participle form look like?
options: always the same as the Perfective
les-32.explain: Participle: y- + stem + -en. Not a personal conjugation — it's a noun-like verb form. wenni [ixeddmen řebda] 'he who always works'.

les-32.q: What changes with ad in a certain relative clause?
les-32.explain: āryaz-enni [d ɣa yasen] 'the man who is to come'. In dependent clauses, ad always becomes ɣa (see also Lesson 10 — explanation §7.1). This also applies to interrogative questions and cleft sentences.
d- = direction element 'this way'. yusin = participle of 'come'. Together: 'the man who came here'.

les-32.q: You want to say "the man I brought here." Which connector do you use?
options: i as relative marker (for DO clauses)
les-32.explain: āryaz [i d-iwyeɣ] 'the man I brought here'. i connects the main word to the subordinate clause if the main word is the direct object.

les-32.correct: de man aan wie ik het gaf
accept: de man aan wie ik het gaf
de man die ik het gaf
les-32.explain: umi = 'to whom' (indirect relation). ṯ-wciɣ = 'I gave it' (clitic fronting). Together: 'the man I gave it to'.

les-32.q: Link type of clause to its characteristic:

pairs.right: dependent clause after it + anaphoric pronoun

les-32.explain: Four patterns. The indefinite/definite distinction is the key principle — then the type of role (subject / DO / IO) chooses which feature the subordinate clause gets.

les-33.q: What is the structure of a cleft sentence?
options: regular VSO phrase with rising intonation
ḏ + emphasized element + i + relative clause
les-33.explain: ḏ baba i d-yiwden 'it is my father who has arrived'. Two parts: (1) ḏ baba = the predicate, (2) i d-yiwden = the relative clause with obligatory marker i.

les-33.q: What do you use a cleft sentence for?
options: for emphasis or contrast — 'it is precisely X that...'
les-33.explain: Neutral message: yus-d baba 'my father has come'. Emphasis: ḏ baba i d-yiwden 'it is MY FATHER who has come' (not anyone else). Classic answer to 'who was that?'.

les-33.correct: het is mijn vader die is aangekomen
accept: het is mijn vader die is aangekomen
mijn vader is het die gekomen is
les-33.explain: ḏ + baba = the predicate. i = relative marker. d-yiwden = 'arrived here'. The cleft structure is similar to French c'est mon père qui est arrivé.

les-33.correct: het is Mimoun die ik zag
accept: het is Mimoun die ik zag
Mimoun is degene die ik zag
les-33.explain: DO cleft: the direct object (Mimun) is emphasized. After i is the subordinate clause where Mimun is the DO — hence clitic fronting: ẓṛiɣ is already there.

les-33.q: What are the two differences between a cleft and a question word question?
options: cleft uses ḏ before and i as connector; query uses neither ḏ nor i
query uses i, cleft does not
cleft is always in the past
les-33.explain: Cleft: ḏ netta i d-yusin. Question: wi d-yusin?. No ḏ, no i in the question. The participle structure of the dependent clause is identical.

les-33.q: How do you say 'it is he who came here'?
les-33.explain: ḏ at the beginning, then the emphasized element (netta), then i, then the dependent clause. Fixed order.

les-33.q:
The ḏ in cleft sentences is the
ḏ for 'and' (between NPs)?
options: no — this is the predicate particle ḏ ('it is')
les-33.explain: Tarifit has written several words as ḏ. In cleft sentences it is the predicate particle 'it is, this is'. In 'necc ḏ uma' it is 'and'. They are always contextually distinct.
The same participle clause (d-yusin) appears in three constructions — but the wrapper determines whether it is a question, emphasis, or DO cleft.

les-34.q: Translation: Ḥenna ṯuɣa ṯessen ijjen wattas n ṯḥuja
les-34.explain: Ḥenna = my grandmother (family word). ṯuɣa = past particle. ṯessen = she knows/knows. ijjen wattas = a lot. n ṯḥuja = of stories.

les-34.q: What function does i have in mamec i ɛeqřeɣ?
options: it is the relative marker — 'how I remember'
les-34.explain: mamec i ɛeqřeɣ = 'how I remember'. mamec is the question word 'how', and i is the relative marker that introduces the clause. A pattern from Lesson 32.

les-34.q: Why is ɣa in i ɣa raḥeɣ instead of ad?
options: in dependent clauses, ad always becomes ɣa
les-34.explain: Fixed rule (Lesson 10 and 32): in relative clauses, interrogative questions and cleft sentences, ad automatically becomes ɣa. Likewise min ɣa negg? 'what shall we do?'.

les-34.q: Translate the dialogue sentence: A ɛli-inu, ma ṯettsed niɣ ɛad waa ṯettised ca?
les-34.correct: mijn Ali, ben je al aan het slapen of nog niet?
accept: mijn Ali ben je al aan het slapen of nog niet?
Ali, slaap je al of nog niet?
les-34.explain: A ɛli-inu = invocation. ma = demand particle. ṯettsed = Imperfective 2SG of sleeping. niɣ = or. ɛad waa...ca = 'not yet'.

les-34.q: The text says degg" xxam — what is this?
options: a contraction of ḏi + wexxam = 'in the room'
les-34.explain: ḏi 'in' + wexxam (related state of axxam 'room') merged into speaking quickly. An example of phonetic assimilation in real spoken language.

les-34.q: How does the boy say 'I'm not sleeping yet'?
les-34.explain: necc = i. ɛad = yet. waa...ca = denial. ttiseɣ = Negative Imperfective 1SG of sleeping.

les-34.q: In wattas n yewdan — which state does yewdan have?
options: connected state — it comes after the preposition n
les-34.explain: After n 'van' always comes connected state (Lesson 15). yewdan is the connected state of 'people'. Free state would be iwdan.

les-34.q: Link text element to its grammatical role:
les-34.explain: A real text combines everything at once. Recognize the blocks: particle + conjunction + negation + preposition + dependent clause marker.

les-35.q: What word traditionally opens a Tarifit fairy tale?
les-35.explain: yekkaa = literally 'it rose' (Perfective of kkaa 'to rise'). As a narrative formula it means 'once upon a time'. Comparable to Dutch 'Once upon a time' or Arabic kan ɣa ma kan.

les-35.q: Translation: Yekkaa ijj uzeǧid ɣaas ijjen yiyyaa n yārḏen yemyaa
les-35.correct: er was eens een koning die een groot tarweveld had
accept: er was eens een koning die een groot tarweveld had
er was een koning met een groot tarweveld
les-35.explain: yekkaa = once upon a time. ijj uzeǧid = one king (joined state after ijj). ɣaas = with him (possession). yiyyaa n yārḏen = wheat field. yemyaa = it was big.

les-35.q: What does the narrative word uca mean?
options: 'then, next' — marks the next step in the story
les-35.explain: uca yus-d zeɛma yemsennaḏ 'then it came to be that it leaned over'. uca is a narrative word that moves the storyline forward — similar to French alors or Arabic ṯumma.

les-35.q: What is the regular opening formula before the actual story?
les-35.explain: Ḥajit-ek — Arabic loanword, literally 'I tell you'. Stands as a ritual announcement before the story. Just like the fairy tale formula in other cultures.

les-35.q: In the sentence uca kkinṯ ssin ṯmeḥtac — what gender/number does kkinṯ have?
les-35.explain: The suffix -enṯ / -ṯ in the Perfective = 3PL:V (they, women). kkinṯ = 'they (women) passed by'. The three reapers are women, hence the feminine plural.

les-35.q: The first reaper begins her wish with mri ḏayi ɣa yawi.... What type of 'if' is this?
options: counterfactual — the situation is not like that (mři)
les-35.explain: mři = 'if (but)' for wishful thinking / counterfactual. The mower dreams of a situation that is not yet reality. mařa would be an open hypothesis that could come true.
zeɛma is an Arabic loanword that in narration distances the speaker from the saying: 'apparently', 'so to speak'. Typical in stories and gossip.

les-35.q: In yemsennaḏ you recognize the prefix m-. What does this indicate?
les-35.explain: yemsennaḏ = 'it hangs over' — the m- is the middle variant of mm- indicating a position or condition. The same prefix as in mřaɣa 'calling each other'.

pairs.right: 'once upon a time' – fairy tale opener
'so to speak' — distance from the speaker

les-35.explain: Tarifit stories have a rich set of narrative words. If you recognize yekkaa and uca, you follow each Tarifit text.

les-36.explain: Imperative of adef 'enter' + direction marker -d 'hither'. Together: 'go in (here)'. Note that the causative was ssidef 'to let in' (Lesson 29).
qa = pseudo-verb locative. -ṯ = he/she/it. ḏi ṯaḏḏarṯ = 'in the house'. Together: 'he/she is home'. Used daily.

les-36.q: You want to offer tea with ma ṯexsed atay?. What do you say when the person says yes?
les-36.explain: aɣ-ac = 'here you have it' (pseudo-verb aɣ + IO suffix -ac 'to you M'). For a woman it would be aɣ-am. Identified in Lesson 05 and Lesson 31.

les-36.q: In the farewell conversation: a nemřaqa, in ca' Allah — what does this mean?
options: we will meet again, Allah willing
les-36.explain: a nemřaqa = 'we will meet each other' (ad + reciprocal mřaqa). in ca' Allah = Arabic 'if God wills'. Together: the standard Riffian farewell greeting.

les-36.q: How do you say 'I'm going to the market'?
les-36.explain: a raḥeɣ = 'I will go' (ad + Aorist, but before r: ad → a). ɣaa ssuq = 'to the market'.
meřmi = when (question word). ɣa = ad in a question word context. ṯeqqebed = 2SG of 'return'. A typically practical question.

les-36.q: The conversation contains ḥamḏullah and baṛakallahu fic. What are these?
options: Arabic expressions that are very common in Tarifit conversations
les-36.explain: Code-switching with Arabic is the norm in Riffian conversations, including among fluent Tarifit speakers. Religious expressions (ḥamḏullah, baṛakallahu, in ca' Allah) are almost always said in Arabic.

les-36.q: At the end of the course: which skill would you best develop further?
options: actively listening to speakers and trying short conversations
les-36.explain: Active input (listening to relatives, Tarifit TV) + output (trying short sentences) is the proven route. The grammar is in there — now it should become automatic.

les-36.q: Link dialogue sentence to its function:

pairs.right: to hand something over (to a man)

les-36.explain: You have completed all 36 lessons. With these sentences you can already function in everyday Riffian conversations. Next step: use them.
